title: How to Roll a Joint: Walkthrough for Beginners
h1: How to Roll a Joint, One Step at a Time
metaDescription: Learn how to roll a joint: supplies, how much flower to use, choosing papers, making a crutch, rolling, sealing and packing, plus fixes and pre-roll options.

body:
Learning how to roll a joint takes a few simple supplies and a little practice: grind your flower, add a crutch, shape the paper, then tuck, roll and seal. Many beginners roll a smokable joint within a few tries, and it gets easier every time. Here's what a joint is, what you'll need, how much flower to use, a step-by-step walkthrough and fixes for the classic mistakes. This guide is for adults 21 and older.

## What a joint is, and how it differs from a blunt or a spliff

A joint is ground cannabis flower rolled in thin rolling paper, usually with a small paper filter, called a crutch, at one end. It's all cannabis and nothing else.

Two cousins are easy to confuse with it:

| | Joint | Blunt | Spliff |
|---|---|---|---|
| Wrapper | Rolling paper | Usually a cigar wrap or tobacco leaf | Rolling paper |
| Filling | Cannabis only | Cannabis | Cannabis mixed with tobacco |
| Tobacco | No | Usually, in the wrap | Yes, in the mix |

Because tobacco brings nicotine with it, blunts and spliffs are a different product from a joint. This guide sticks to the all-cannabis version.

Two more terms you'll hear: the **crutch**, or tip, is the filter at the mouth end, and the **roach** is the small end left when a joint is finished. The crutch keeps that end firm, keeps flower out of your mouth and makes the last part easier to hold.

## Supplies: flower, grinder, papers and crutch material

You don't need much:

- **Cannabis flower.** Start with about half a gram per joint.
- **A grinder.** It breaks flower into an even, fluffy texture. Scissors or fingers work in a pinch, but less evenly. Two-piece grinders simply grind, while models with more pieces add a chamber for the ground flower, and many add a screen that collects kief, the fine, resin-rich dust that falls from the buds. Either works for rolling.
- **Rolling papers.** A medium-thickness paper is easiest to learn on. More on choosing them below.
- **Crutch material.** Pre-cut filter tips, or thin, plain cardstock. Skip glossy or printed paper, which isn't meant to be heated near your mouth.
- **Optional extras.** A rolling tray to catch stray flower, a pen or poker to pack the end, and a rolling machine if your hands need help.

Michigan's adult-use law lets adults 21 and older buy and use accessories like these. High Society's menus include an accessories category, and selection varies by store. Our [guide to cannabis accessories](/blog/guide-to-cannabis-accessories/) covers grinders, trays and more.

## How much weed goes in a joint?

Less than most people think. Researchers who analyzed more than 10,000 U.S. cannabis purchases estimated the average joint at about 0.31 to 0.32 grams. Other studies put typical joints at 0.3 to 0.5 grams.

| Joint | Flower | Good for |
|---|---|---|
| Slim | About 0.3 g | A short session for one |
| Standard | About 0.5 g | One or two people |
| Large | 0.75 to 1 g | Sharing with a group |

For a first try, half a gram in a 1 1/4 paper is a forgiving combination: enough flower to shape, not so much that the paper bulges. At that size, an eighth, or 3.5 grams, rolls about seven joints.

## Picking flower for rolling

The flower itself makes rolling easier or harder:

- **Moisture.** Look for buds that feel springy, not damp and not crumbly. Bone-dry flower grinds to dust and burns hot and fast. Damp flower clumps, struggles to stay lit and can leave a soggy seam.
- **Grind.** Aim for a medium, even texture, a bit like loose-leaf tea. Powder packs too tightly, and chunks leave air pockets.
- **Cleanup.** Pick out stems and seeds before grinding. Stems poke holes in the paper, and seeds pop when they burn.
- **Strain.** Any flower you enjoy will roll. Choose by aroma and the experience you're after.

A quick moisture check: bend a small stem. If it snaps cleanly, the flower is dry enough to grind well. If it bends without breaking, it's on the damp side and may clump. Keeping flower in an airtight jar helps it stay in that middle ground.

Our guide to [cannabis flower](/blog/cannabis-flower-101/) explains how to read strain types, potency and aroma.

## Picking rolling papers: size, material and thickness

### Size

- **Single wide:** the shortest and narrowest, for slim joints.
- **1 1/4:** a little longer and wider, a comfortable middle size for half-gram joints.
- **King size:** long and roomy, for large joints meant for sharing.

### Material

- **Wood pulp:** easy to handle, a little thicker.
- **Hemp:** slightly textured, with good grip.
- **Rice:** very thin, with little paper taste, but slippery to handle.
- **Flax:** thin and smooth.

Unbleached papers are brown, and bleached papers are white. Thinner papers add less paper flavor, while thicker ones are more forgiving while you learn.

### Thickness

Start with a medium paper. Once your tuck and roll feel steady, try a thinner one and see whether you notice the difference in taste.

## How to roll a joint in seven steps

Here's how to make a joint by hand, from loose flower to a sealed, packed joint.

1. **Grind.** Grind about half a gram to a medium, even texture.
2. **Make the crutch.** Cut a strip of cardstock about 1 inch wide and 2 to 3 inches long. Fold the first half inch into a few small accordion pleats, like a W or an M, then wrap the rest of the strip around the folds into a firm cylinder.
3. **Fill.** Hold the paper with the glue strip along the top edge, facing you, and crease it lightly down the middle. Set the crutch at one end and sprinkle flower evenly along the crease, leaving a little room at the far end.
4. **Shape.** Pinch the paper between your thumbs and index fingers and roll it back and forth to pack the flower into an even cylinder. This is where the joint's final shape is decided, so take your time.
5. **Tuck.** Using your thumbs, tuck the edge without glue under the flower, starting at the crutch end. It's the hardest step. A firm, even tuck makes everything after it easy. If the paper won't catch, steady the flower with your index fingers while your thumbs push the front edge under and around it.
6. **Roll and seal.** Roll upward until only the glue strip shows, moisten it lightly and press it down along the whole length.
7. **Pack the end.** Tap the crutch end gently on the table, then pack the open end with a pen tip or poker. Top it up with a pinch of flower if needed and twist the tip closed.

### How to roll a cone

A cone is wide at the lit end and narrow at the crutch. To roll one, angle the paper slightly as you tuck, keeping the crutch end snug while the far end flares out. Fill it gradually, packing as you go. You can also buy pre-rolled cones: drop in flower, pack it gently with a poker and twist the top closed.

## Practice tips for rolling a joint for beginners

Rolling a joint for beginners is mostly about repetition. A few habits shorten the learning curve:

- **Start with small fills.** A quarter gram is easier to shape than a full gram while you learn the tuck.
- **Work over a tray.** It catches stray flower, so nothing goes to waste, and gives you a clean surface.
- **Make crutches ahead.** Fold a few at once, so each practice roll can focus on the paper.
- **Slow down at the tuck.** Rushing the tuck is the usual reason a joint comes out loose or lumpy. If it isn't catching, unroll and try again.
- **Try a rolling machine.** A simple roller shapes and tucks for you: load the flower, close it, spin the rollers, then feed in the paper and seal. It's a good bridge while your hands learn.
- **Expect a few lumpy ones.** Everyone's first joints look a little rough. They still work, and the next one will look better.

## Tips and common mistakes

- **Canoeing.** When one side burns faster than the other, the joint canoes. It usually starts with uneven packing, a damp spot from the seal or lighting just one side. Hold the flame just below the tip and turn the joint slowly until the whole end glows evenly. If one side races ahead anyway, pause and let the burn even out.
- **Too loose.** A loose joint burns fast, drops embers and can come apart. Pack more firmly while shaping, and tamp the end.
- **Too tight.** A tight joint is hard to draw from. Roll it gently between your fingers to loosen it, or unroll it and start over with a looser shape.
- **Runs.** A run is a streak of burning racing up one side, often from a weak seam. Press the seam firmly along its full length when you seal.
- **Soaked glue.** Too much moisture on the glue strip wrinkles or tears the paper. A light touch is enough.
- **Overfilling.** An overfilled paper is hard to tuck. Start with less flower than you think you need.
- **Going out.** Joints often go out between puffs, and that's normal. Tap off the ash and relight the end evenly.
- **Storing extras.** A rolled joint dries out faster than whole buds. Keep extras in a small airtight tube or jar, away from heat and light, and where kids and pets can't reach them.

Wherever you roll, light up only where it's allowed. Michigan doesn't allow cannabis use in public places, property owners can ban it on their property, and smoking isn't allowed in a vehicle's passenger area on a public road.

## No time to roll? Pre-rolls and cones

If rolling isn't for you, there are two easy shortcuts:

- **Pre-rolls.** These ready-made joints come in full-gram, half-gram and mini sizes, often in multipacks, and licensed packages list their net weight. Infused pre-rolls add concentrate to the flower and are much stronger, so check the THC on the label.
- **Pre-rolled cones.** Empty cones with a crutch already in place. Grind, fill, pack and twist.

A pre-roll is the easier pick when you want a consistent size every time or you're sharing from a multipack. It also lets you sample a few strains without buying an eighth of each. Cones suit anyone who likes choosing their own flower but would rather skip the tuck.

High Society's menus include pre-rolls, and selection varies by store. Browse your store's [menu](/shop/), compare sizes in our [pre-roll buyer's guide](/blog/pre-roll-buyers-guide/) and learn more about [mini pre-rolls](/blog/mini-pre-rolls/). Prefer a pipe? Here's [how to pack a bowl](/blog/how-to-pack-a-bowl/). Recreational shopping is available to individuals 21 years or older. Enjoy cannabis responsibly.

faq.q: How much weed goes in a joint?
faq.a: Usually 0.3 to 0.5 grams. Researchers who analyzed more than 10,000 U.S. purchases estimated the average joint at about a third of a gram. Beginners often find half a gram in a 1 1/4 paper easiest to roll, while a full gram makes a large joint better suited to sharing.

A crutch is a small rolled filter of stiff paper at the mouth end of a joint, also called a tip. It gives the joint structure, keeps flower out of your mouth and makes the end easier to hold. Use pre-cut tips or plain, thin cardstock, and skip glossy or printed paper.

faq.q: Why does my joint burn unevenly?
faq.a: Usually because the flower is packed unevenly. A damp spot from sealing, a stray stem or lighting only one side can also start a canoe, where one side burns ahead. Grind evenly, shape carefully before you tuck, use a light touch on the glue and rotate the joint as you light it.

faq.q: Which papers are best for beginners?
faq.a: Medium-thickness 1 1/4 papers are a forgiving place to start. They're wide enough to hold half a gram without crowding, and thick enough to handle without tearing. Once your rolling is steady, try thinner hemp or rice papers, which add less paper taste but take a lighter touch.
